title: Draft: builds, a predicted winrate and a multisearch

items.text: Builds for this draft: each of your picks gets its most played finished items in that role, in order, with that build's winrate, then adjusted for the enemy team. Anti-heal goes to one player against healers (two against three or more: the ADC first, then another physical carry, then a mage), boots change for heavy AD, heavy AP, crowd control or slows, and one defensive item is added where it answers something specific, like Zhonya's against divers or Mercurial Scimitar against suppression. Each change says why.
A predicted winrate for the draft, updating as picks go in: every pick on both sides gets the same expected winrate the suggestions use, and the two sides' average picks are set against each other.

Multisearch: paste the enemy's Riot IDs (or their joined-the-lobby lines) and press Search. Each is looked up live with Riot: solo and flex rank with winrate, the last ten ranked games (record, KDA, roles), top champion masteries, and the three champions they are most likely to pick, plus anything the group's own games know about them. It shows how long a search will take and how much of the site's Riot allowance it uses, and if the allowance runs low it pauses with a countdown and carries on by itself.

Pick suggestions are steadier: the player's own record leans more on the champion's usual winrate when it rests on a handful of games, and the ally, enemy and lane adjustments together are held to a few points, so one lucky pairing cannot push a pick to the top.

Choosing red side in the Draft tab no longer moves your team across the board. Your team stays on the left and the enemy on the right; the side you choose only decides whether you have first pick (blue) or second pick (red).

Your team's pick order in the Draft tab is now set by dragging: pick a row up by its ⠿ handle and the other rows slide out of its way as you move it, so what you see is the order you will get; let go and it settles into place. A finger works too, or focus the handle and use the arrow keys. Rows that have already picked stay where they are.

Matchups on each profile's Champions tab: pick any champion the player has three or more games on (and the role, if they play it in more than one) to see every lane opponent they have faced, with their record, lane gold at 15 minutes and KDA, beside how everyone in the stored lobbies does in the same matchup, plus their best and worst matchups. Each champion card links straight to its matchups.

Fill the draft from a screenshot: in champion select, take a screenshot of the client window (Alt+Print Screen) and paste it on the Draft tab with Ctrl+V, or drop it in. Both teams' picks and bans are read from the champion icons, your lanes are guessed from your champions, and you check what was found before it fills the board. It runs in your browser; the screenshot is never uploaded.

title: Rings of fire, new records, and a proper draft board

items.text: A game score of 90 or more is now ringed in blue flame all the way round, the way Overwatch set a portrait on fire.

Account pictures on the Overview catch fire on a streak: green flames for three solo wins in a row and gold, shining, for ten. Three losses in a row turns them to smoke, and ten to a dark red fire. The streak is shown beside the last ten games too.

This week gains Climber of the week (most Solo/Duo LP since Monday), Promoted (anyone who went up a division or tier), Best game of the week, Grinder (most games) and New pick (a champion played for the first time this season, and how it went).
New records: On fire (most games scored 90+), Best day (most LP in one day), Champion pool (most different champions) and One-trick (biggest share of games on one champion).
New single-game bests: Speedrun (fastest win), Marathon game (longest game), Farmer (most CS) and Main character (highest share of the team's damage).
Comeback specialist now goes to whoever comes back from 5k+ behind in the biggest share of their games, rather than the most comebacks in total.

Draft suggestions have a Blind safety score from 0 to 100: how safe a champion is to pick before you see the enemy laner. It rewards steady lane gold whoever it faces, little chance of meeting a counter that is still available (banned or already picked counters drop out) and still winning from behind. It moves the order most for the first pick and not at all once the enemy laner is known. A warning chip names the worst lane still open.

The Draft tab is now a draft board: blue on the left, red on the right, the same size, with five bans and five picks for each side in the order they are made. The slot that is up is highlighted and a strip along the top shows the whole sequence.
Two formats: Ranked draft (all ten bans at once, then B1 · R1 R2 · B2 B3 · R3 R4 · B4 B5 · R5) and Ranked 5s, the tournament draft with a second ban phase after the first six picks.

Each enemy pick's lane is guessed from how often that champion plays each role, all five together so two picks never share a lane. Set a lane by hand to override it. The guessed laner is used for the lane matchup.
The suggested pick order now only moves the players still to pick, and puts first anyone whose enemy laner is already showing, since they can answer it whenever they pick.

title: A draft helper, champions to learn, and a pick-versus-win chart

items.text: Draft: a new tab for champion select. Put yourselves in pick order (it can suggest one: fewest strong champions picks first, the deepest pool last), fill in the enemy as they lock in, and get suggestions for each pick from your own games on the champion, how it has done beside your locked picks and against theirs, and the lane matchup.

Each profile's Roles & classes tab now suggests champions to learn in that role: strong in lobbies near your rank, sharing a class with what you already play, and rarely picked or banned, so you can count on getting them.
Champions has a Pick vs win view: every champion placed by winrate against pick rate, ringed by ban rate, with hidden gems, underachievers and the most banned listed underneath.
Bans are now recorded with each game. Older games are being fetched again for theirs, so ban rates fill in over the next day or so.
Rank change by game now plots your rank after each game on the same scale as Daily rank, and both charts have each tier's colour behind them again.
The last-ten-games strip on each account card now reads newest first, left to right.
A game score of 90 or more shows in blue with small flames: better than nine in ten games for that role and rank.
The champion lists can be sorted by games or winrate as well as A to Z: use the Sort buttons or click a column heading.
A game score could differ by a fraction of a point between the site and the page that explains it when a number fell exactly on a fraction like one third. Both now round the same way.

title: A tab icon

items.text: The site now has its own icon in the browser tab: the L from the header, on its blue-to-teal tile.

title: A new layout: one site, a page for each of you, and a page for each champion

items.text: The Basic and Data halves are now one site. Across the top: Overview, Champions, Roles & classes, Time patterns, Duos & stacks, Game flow and Records. The old one-page layout is still there as Classic view, linked at the bottom of every page, and old links send you to the right place.

Every player has a profile: rank card, predicted LP for the next win and loss, and tabs for Overview, Champions, Roles & classes, Roaming, Time patterns, Duos & stacks, Game flow and Records. Open one from the search box in the header or by clicking a name.

A profile's Overview lists every game as a bar: champion, level, spells, runes, KDA, kill share, CS, vision, lobby rank, score, items and the LP it moved. Open one for both scoreboards, laning, objectives and builds, or go on to the full game breakdown.

Ranked panels on each profile: rank change game by game for each queue, daily rank, LP gained on each champion, and an MMR panel comparing LP per win and per loss over the season and the last 50 games. MMR is shown as above, around or below your rank with the gap, and is an estimate.

Predicted LP now uses only games whose LP change was measured on its own, leaves out remakes, weights the last 15 wins and 15 losses so recent ones count most, and says 'not enough games' below five. Where there are too few it falls back to the old estimate.

Champions has an index grouped by role or by class, with rank, patch and group-or-everyone filters, and every champion has a page: overall record, winrate by patch, counters (30 games or more), averages by rank, and how each of you does on it.
The Overview front page shows everyone's ranked accounts, rank charts, the last 24 hours, the group's top 10 champions and a This week panel.
Records gains single-game bests, top three each: most healing and shielding on allies, highest vision score, most kills, most damage to champions and highest game score.
Games are being fetched again for item, spell and rune detail. Game bars show them as each game is reached.

title: The checklist: game scores, ranks, jungle pathing, records, and a drawn map

items.text: Every game now has a score from 0 to 100. It is built from up to ten numbers: six for the role, two for the champion's class and up to two for its tags, weighted 60 / 25 / 15. Each is a percentile against players in the same role at the same rank, so 50 is an ordinary game for that role at that level. Open any game in Game breakdown to see the score for all ten players and, for one of you, every number behind it.

Top champions are ranked by a new score in place of Performance: the average game score on that champion, weighted by the rank it was played at, by how many games there are (full weight at fifty) and by whether you win more than that champion usually does at your rank. Click a champion in either top champions table to see the working, step by step.

Ranks. The site now reads the rank of all ten players when a game is collected, and is working back through the season's games as well. Riot only ever says what a rank is today, so older games get today's rank; from here on each game keeps the rank it was played at. This is what lets a Gold support be compared with Gold supports. Until a game has been reached, everyone in it is placed at the rank of whichever of you played it, and the top of the page says how far the catch-up has got.
Players: radars by rank (your line against the average for your role at each rank), winrate by lobby rank, and the games-by-mode and roles-played donuts and winrate by queue from the original site.

Jungle pathing on the Players tab for anyone who jungles: the camp you start on (read at 1:00, five seconds after camps appear), your usual route to 4:00, how often you full clear and how long it takes, how often you gank before finishing and whether it works, how the first two scuttles go, and every jungler in the group side by side.

A Records tab: the season highlights from the Basic page, plus new ones from the minute-by-minute data such as biggest comeback and throw, thief, robbed, fastest first item, furthest roam and who holds up best after two losses.

Champions opens on a grid of every champion the group has played, grouped by class, with a proper search that suggests as you type. A champion's page now shows each matchup three ways: how the champion does against it across every stored game, then each of you beside that, coloured by who beats it and who falls short.

Duos has a second view, Champion pairs with randoms: pick one of your champions and see every teammate's champion in a given role, friend or stranger, with the winrate against your usual and by class. For example, which supports your ADC does best with in solo queue.

The map is drawn by the site again, from the group's own flat copy of the minimap, in place of the image. Positions, kill participation, kills, assists and deaths are separate switches on both maps, so positions can be seen on their own. Jungle and roaming views use a second colouring that picks out only the river and the jungle.

Roaming counts the river in two halves and the jungle as yours and theirs. The bar shows one block each for river and jungle, biggest first; point at a block (or tap it) for the split and the average at your rank. Does roaming pay off now shows the gold difference at 15 for every lane, not just two.

Data analysis merges each person's second account into their first by default, so nobody is split in two. Show second accounts in the header brings them back. The Basic page is unchanged, because a rank belongs to an account.
Champion classes and tags are now the League of Legends Wiki's, kept in one file and credited in the footer. A champion shows its class once, and its tags beside it.

Throws and comebacks count from 5k gold, up from 3k, and are judged on a win chance that knows how each team's champions scale: a team of late champions that was behind at 15 and expected to win anyway is not a comeback. Game flow has a switch between gold only and gold plus team scaling, and a table of which champions do better later.
One set of game phases everywhere: laning to 15 minutes, mid game to 25, late after.
Time patterns shows all 24 hours from 5am. Click a bar in the session chart, or 7+, for every game number up to 15 and beyond with its winrate, gold and deaths.

Small samples. A cell with under five games no longer gets a red or green background, an average over under ten is greyed, and nothing is called best or worst on fewer than thirty: the best and worst time to queue for one player could come from thirteen games before.

Who fades in long sessions uses one rule for everybody: ten sessions that reached a fifth game. Anyone short of that is listed underneath with their count, where before one person was left out without a word and another got a line through four points.
The duo synergy grid fits its card. With eleven accounts the last two columns sat off the edge and looked missing.

On Roles and classes, picking a class changes the two comparison rows and what the cells are coloured against. Junglers are compared on their share of objective damage, since every jungler is part of nearly every objective. Radars have no dashed lines. Charts fill their cards. Wide tables scroll sideways on a phone with the first column held in place.

Two things on the list turned out not to be bugs. There are no trios because no game this season has exactly three tracked accounts on a team: it is always solo, duo or a five, and the fours are fives with one account the site does not follow. And the minus signs on bot lane gold at 15 are real: the group's ADCs are behind at 15 more often than not and win later. Both cards now say so.
The pages use the full width of a big screen instead of stopping short of it, and rows that were sitting flush against each other have their spacing back.

Champions are grouped by the League wiki's subclasses: Enchanter, Catcher, Warden, Vanguard, Juggernaut, Diver, Skirmisher, Assassin, Burst mage, Battlemage, Artillery, Marksman, Specialist. The older parent classes the wiki also keeps (Controller, Fighter, Slayer and so on) are gone, because they say less about what a champion actually does.

Solo and duo are counted apart on the Players tab, in both the games-by-mode donut and the winrate by mode. Riot calls them one queue, so duo means another tracked account was on the team: a duo with someone the site does not follow still counts as solo.

The game-number pop-up on Time patterns shows every game number out to 20 and beyond, games 1 to 10 down one side and 11 up the other, each with its winrate, lane gold and deaths. It used to stop at 15.
The day-and-hour heatmap writes the hours out in full, 5AM and 12PM rather than 5A and 12P.
Roles on the Players tab are in map order, top to support, instead of being shuffled by how much each is played. It still opens on the role you actually play.
Top champions on the Basic page lists five rather than six.

The top champions working said a score was weighted at the rank you were "mostly" playing. The score always weighted each game at its own rank; the page now says so and lists the ranks those games were played at.

title: Real icons, the real map, and a face you can choose

items.text: Pick your own icon. Everyone is shown as a champion portrait, which starts as the champion you have the most mastery on. Click the portrait on your player card, or at the top of the Players tab in Data analysis, and choose any champion: your most played are listed first and there is a search for the rest. The choice is kept in your browser, so it is how you see that person, and it follows you between the two halves of the site.

The game map is the actual minimap now instead of a drawing of one, and in the Positions view every player is their champion's portrait, ringed blue or red for their team and in their own colour if they are one of you.

The map plays. Press play and the game runs back at about forty times speed, or drag the bar to any five seconds of it. Riot only records where everyone stands once a minute, plus the exact spot of each death, so movement between those points is drawn as a straight line and anyone who has just died stays where they fell, faded, until the next sample.

Objectives look like what they are. Each drake has its own element's icon, and grubs, heralds, barons, Atakhan and elder have theirs, on the gold chart and in the objective log, ringed by which team took it. Roles have their icons beside them wherever a role is named.

The analysis now covers the whole season. It launched yesterday on about four games in ten while the rest were still being fetched; every game is in now, so the percentiles, the win-chance model and the lobby averages are standing on all of it.

title: Data analysis: a second half of the site

items.text: There are two modes now, switched from beside the title. Basic is the dashboard you know. Data analysis is new, and it is built on something the site never had before: every player in every one of your games, not only you, plus what happened minute by minute. That is what lets it say whether your vision score is good for a support in your lobbies rather than just what it is.

Game breakdown. Any game opens to its full scoreboard, the team gold lead through the game with every dragon, herald and baron marked on it, each lane's gold, XP and CS difference at 10 and 15, a win chance that moves with the gold, the objective log with who killed and who helped, and a map you can scrub through to see every kill or where all ten players stood at any minute.

Players. Pick a role and get six stats that matter for that role with a percentile against everyone else who played it in your games, a radar, a map of where you stand, kill and die in each phase of the game, how often your early takedowns happen away from your own lane and whether your games go better when they do.

Champions, Roles and classes, Time patterns, Duos and stacks, Game flow. Who plays a champion best and what they build on it. Winrate by champion class for each of you. Winrate by day and hour, by game number in a sitting, and after a loss. Winrate by how many of you were on the team, by role pairing and by champion pairing. And how often a lead at 15 is actually converted, with each person's throws and comebacks.

On the Overview: every game from the last 24 hours as a card that opens its breakdown, and three new lines in This week at a glance for who took part in the most objectives, who roamed most, and how the group does after midnight.

Top champions are ranked by Performance now, here and on each player's card. It is half winrate, held toward 50% until there are enough games to believe it, and half how those games rank against the lobby in that role, so six wins from six no longer sits above sixty from a hundred. Each champion also says whether it is a Main, Comfortable or still Learning by how much it is played.

Each player's card has their average gold difference at 15 against their lane opponent and their kill participation beside the lobby's, and every recent game lists its gold at 15 with a link straight to the breakdown.
The tabs are reordered to Overview, Players, Duos, Rank progress, Records, the Friends tab is called Players, and the page is wider so the leaderboard and the week sit side by side.

Three honest limits. Full detail arrives a few hundred games at a time, newest first, so the analysis says how many of the season's games it is built from until it has them all. Ward positions are not in what Riot provides, so the map shows kills and positions only. And a stolen objective is only labelled when it cannot be anything else.

title: James has a second account now

items.text: James2nd joins as James's second account, which makes eleven players and four second accounts. The switch in the header that hides second accounts now hides four, and with it off the board is back to the seven of you on your mains.

An eleventh colour. The palette had exactly ten slots for ten players, and an eleventh would have been dropped off both rank charts rather than drawn. James2nd is a lighter version of James's orchid, the same way the other three pairs work. This one was the awkward one: a pale orchid sits right between Neel's violet and Shas2nd's pale pink, and washed out it reads as whichever of the two it happens to sit beside, so it keeps the purple and only gains lightness. Checked by measuring it against every other colour rather than by eye.

title: Kirish renamed both his accounts, and the site now copes with that

items.text: Kirish renamed both of his accounts on 1 November. Riot looks accounts up by name, so both stopped resolving that morning, and the whole dashboard froze there: the fetch refuses to write a file that would silently drop a player, so nobody's data had updated in five days. Both are pointing at the right accounts again and his history is intact, because none of it was ever filed under the old names.

A rename no longer breaks anything. The id Riot actually identifies an account by never changes, and the fetch log has been keyed by it since the first run, so when a name stops resolving the fetch looks the account up by that id instead, picks the new name up from Riot and carries on. The name in the config is only a starting point now.

A problem that lasts is reported once a day instead of once every fifteen minutes. This one sent about 460 identical failure emails for a single thing that needed saying once. The page is also held back while a fetch is failing rather than being redeployed unchanged, so the build time on the page always means the data behind it is that fresh.

title: Kirish has a second account now

items.text: Kirish's second account joins as Kirish2nd, marked as Kirish's second account, so the switch in the header that hides second accounts now hides three: his, Brett's and Shas's.

A tenth colour. The palette had exactly nine slots for nine players and a tenth would have been dropped from both charts. Kirish2nd is a lighter version of Kirish's blue, the same way the other two pairs work, with the care being Rory: he holds a greyed blue already, so this one stays saturated and goes pale, and the three read as three rather than as Rory twice. Checked at the width a chart line is drawn.

title: Season highlights moves to a Records tab

items.text: Season highlights has a tab of its own called Records, between Duo synergy and Friends. It was the last thing on the Overview, under the leaderboard, the group totals, the champion table and the week at a glance, which is a long way to scroll for the part people actually enjoy.
The tab only appears when there is something to put in it, the same way Duo synergy does, and it has its own address, so a link ending in records opens straight to it.

title: The rings answer to a tap

items.text: Game types and Roles played could only be read with a mouse. A ring answers in its own hole when you hover a segment, and a phone has nothing to hover with; tapping an SVG shape does not reliably focus it either, so on a phone the two rings were decoration. They answer to a tap now, and tapping away puts the title back.

Where there is no pointer, each ring says Tap a segment underneath. On a mouse you find out a ring is interactive by moving across it, which is why the prompt only appears where that cannot happen. No legend: a legend is a second copy of the same figures, takes more room than the ring it explains, and makes you match colours by eye.

title: The Friends tab opens as a list, and the trend column says the number first

items.text: With everybody showing, the friend cards fold down to a header: name, rank, peak, seven-day trend and the last ten games. Nine full seasons end to end was several screens of scrolling to find one person, and the buttons above already do the finding. Click any card, or any name, to open that season in full.

The seven-day trend is a figure with a destination under it rather than one running sentence. It was the widest column in the table and the least scannable, because the number you came for was buried mid-paragraph. The approximate marker is a footnote beside the figure now instead of sitting at the end of the line looking like a typo.

The duo matrix keeps its names on screen. Nine players across and nine down is wider and taller than the window, and the moment the header row scrolled away every cell became an unlabelled percentage.
The tab strip no longer cuts Friends in half on a phone. Rank progress and Duo synergy are Ranks and Duos at that width, and all four fit without scrolling.

title: The dashboard gets its shape back, starting with the phone

items.text: The leaderboard is no longer a six-column table on a phone. It used to overflow into a sideways scroll, which put winrate, record and the seven-day trend off the right-hand edge behind a gesture nobody makes: the three things the table exists to tell you were the three you could not see. Each player is a small block now, name and rank on top, the numbers underneath, nothing hidden.

The header is one row. Platform, freshness, season and key expiry used to be four pill-shaped chips sitting directly under the title; on a phone they wrapped to four lines and pushed the first real number most of a screen down. They are one quiet line of small print now, and the five buttons sit on a single row instead of wrapping and stranding the last one on its own.

Panels look like panels. The page, a panel and a row inside it used to sit within about ten levels of lightness of each other, so nothing read as being on top of anything and the whole dashboard looked like one flat sheet with text on it. There is a proper scale behind it now, a visible edge on each panel, and one spacing rhythm rather than a hand-picked gap per element.

title: Brett has a second account now

items.text: Brett's second account joins as Brett2nd, marked as Brett's second account. The switch in the header that hides second accounts now hides both his and Shas's, and every number on the page is recalculated without them.

A ninth colour, because the palette had exactly eight and a ninth player would have been dropped from both charts with an apologetic note underneath. Brett2nd is a softer version of Brett's orange for the same reason Shas2nd is a softer pink: the pair should read as one person with two accounts rather than two strangers. Checked at the width a chart line is actually drawn, which is where two similar colours stop being two colours.

title: A switch for second accounts

items.text: A switch in the header that takes second accounts off the dashboard. Shas2nd is the one marked at the moment, so turning it on leaves the six primary accounts. It is not a filter over the top: every number is recalculated without them, so the leaderboard renumbers, the group totals drop, the combined winrate and the champion count move, pairs involving a second account disappear from duo synergy, and both charts lose the line. The switch keeps you on the tab you were reading.
Which accounts count as second accounts is set in the config rather than guessed from the name, because Riot has no idea that two accounts belong to one person and nothing in the data says so.

Technically this is a second copy of the whole page rather than something the browser switches off. Every figure on the dashboard is worked out when the page is built, so hiding a player in the browser would mean writing all of that arithmetic a second time in another language, and the two would drift. Building the page twice costs a few seconds and is right by construction.
Past release notes still name second accounts where they always did. Those are a record of what changed and when, not live data, and editing them to match a switch would make them untrue.

title: Brett is orange

items.text: Brett's colour is orange, and Rory goes back to the steel blue he had before. The two sit next to each other in every legend and only one of them can be warm: at the width a chart line is drawn, two warm colours are one colour with a bit of shading, and the two lines read as one player having a mixed week. So the orange moves rather than being shared.

title: Clicking a name can isolate instead of hide, and the ladder stops at Challenger

items.text: A switch above the LP per game chart for what clicking a name in the key does. Click to hide takes that person off, which is what you want when the chart is crowded. Click to isolate leaves only them, which is what you want when you are trying to follow one line out of eight. Clicking an isolated player again puts everyone back. The daily chart's key follows the same switch, and the two keep their own state so switching one does not rearrange the other.

With one player showing, the chart rescales to them. Both axes are rebuilt from whoever is left rather than the lines simply being hidden, so an Emerald player is no longer a flat scribble along the bottom of an axis still stretched to fit somebody three tiers above them.

A view zoomed inside a single tier names its own divisions. There is no tier line in shot to read them against, and a lone I does not say which tier's I it is, so it reads Emerald I rather than I. A range narrow enough to fall between two division lines is widened to the ones either side, so there is always a horizontal reference.

The chart no longer draws ranks that do not exist. The projection is a random walk and over a few hundred games it wandered far past Challenger, dragging the top of the axis with it: the real lines were squashed into a smudge along the bottom and the tier labels read Challenger six times over, once per 400 points of nowhere. The walk now flattens at Challenger, which is the truth of it, and the axis stops there. A genuine Challenger would still get an axis tall enough to hold them.

title: Rory is orange

items.text: Rory's colour is orange, on the charts, the legends and everywhere else his name is coloured. He was a pale steel blue before.

Brett takes the steel Rory left. His copper and Rory's orange sit next to each other in every legend, and at the width a chart line is actually drawn the two are one colour with a bit of shading, which makes two players' lines read as one. Trying to separate them by making one vivid and the other earthy did not survive being looked at. Moving Brett to a cool colour leaves exactly one warm line on the page, which makes it unmistakably Rory's.

title: The pit of shame

items.text: Whoever is last on the ladder gets their own line under the row of names on the Friends tab, centred, in red, labelled PIT OF SHAME. Picking them still works the same way, and selecting them keeps the red rather than promoting them back to the ordinary blue.

It goes by place rather than by where the sort happened to leave people, so two players level on the bottom both go in rather than one of them being picked arbitrarily. If everybody is level, or there is only one player, there is no bottom to be at and no pit is drawn.

title: James joins, and the page stops falling over when somebody has no rank

items.text: James is on the dashboard. He has no ranked standing in any queue at the moment, so he shows as Unranked and sits at the bottom of the leaderboard, and he is left off the LP per game chart until he has a rank for his games to be measured against. His season history is all there on his card.

Adding him broke the build outright. The row of name buttons asked for each player's Solo/Duo tier and fell back to an empty record when they had none, but that fallback was written inside a template where braces start an expression rather than escaping, so it read as a set containing an empty record and raised unhashable type: dict. It could only ever run for somebody with no Solo/Duo rank, so it sat there harmlessly until the first unranked friend arrived.

title: A game played over midnight no longer disappears

items.text: Kirish's game at 12:59 AM was missing from Rank progress, and would have stayed missing. A reading is taken when somebody has played since their last one, and that was being judged on when the game started. This game started at 11:59 PM, a couple of minutes before the reading taken at midnight, and finished at 12:27 AM, well after it. By its start it looked older than the reading, so no new reading was ever written; by its finish it was newer, and the midnight reading could not contain its LP. The game fell between the two and never appeared.

The question is now asked about when the game finished, which is the same correction made to how the chart files games. The reading lands on the next hour once the result has settled, and the game turns up with its real LP. It is the same mistake in two places: a game is not an instant, it is half an hour, and which side of a reading it falls on depends on which end you ask about.

title: A game belongs to the hour it finished in

items.text: Per-game LP was being shared out against the wrong readings. Games were filed by when they started, and a game lasts half an hour, so one beginning at 16:33 and ending at 17:04 was counted against the reading taken at 17:02, which could not possibly contain it. Its LP then landed on whichever games came next. That is why some wins read +6 and +7 while the losses around them paid for them.

Games are filed by when they finished, which is when LP actually moves. Kirish's run of wins on 14 September reads +20 each now instead of +6, +7 and +6, and his two losses before them are -21 rather than -10 and -11. Across the whole season this takes the games sitting in a stretch that moved less than half of what it should from 28 down to 3.
A game that finished after the most recent reading waits for the reading that includes it, rather than being given a made-up value now. It appears on the next refresh with its real number.

title: Readings the games contradict are no longer believed

items.text: Some games were worth 0 LP and the ones after them were worth double. Four of Brett's losses on 15 September read 0, 0, -34 and -34 when every one of them was about -17. The reading taken between them said his LP was unchanged after two defeats, which cannot be true of two defeats: one game was still being played and the other had finished minutes earlier than Riot's ranked entry had noticed. The chart treated that reading as measured fact and charged the next two games for it.

The games now get a say. Wins raise LP and losses lower it, always, so a run of nothing but wins that did not gain, or nothing but losses that did not lose, has a boundary that had not caught up, and it is dropped. The segment runs on to the next reading that the games do not contradict. Nothing is invented: every reading left is still a measurement, there is just one fewer of them. Brett's four losses now read -17 each and land exactly on the rank he was measured at.

A reading is also no longer taken while a game is still settling. If somebody has a game in progress, or one that finished in the last ten minutes, that queue is skipped for the hour and picked up on the next one. Nothing is lost by waiting, and the reading is worth having only once it can answer where they actually stand.

This came in with the change to recording a reading whenever somebody played. The rule before it kept a reading only when the number moved, which threw these away by accident. Keeping them is right, since they are real measurements, and the fix belongs where the chart decides what a measurement means rather than in what gets written down.

title: Everything reads from the one log now

items.text: The daily chart, the seven-day trend and every rank figure on the page are built from the readings log rather than from the separate daily file. The daily view of it is worked out from the log when the page is built: a day's anchor is the reading written as its anchor, and the day's last reading is the other half, which is exactly what the old file held. Nothing on the page had to learn about any of this, and nothing about it moved.

The LP per game chart now uses every reading in the log, including the end-of-day ones carried over from the old file. Those are real measurements of somebody's rank at a known time, and each one is another point where the graph knows what the rank actually was rather than sharing one measured change between more games. Expect slightly different per-game numbers on the older stretches, and better ones.

The old daily file is still written, and the build compares what it derives against it every time and says whether they agree. It is the one thing here Riot cannot re-serve, so it keeps being written until that comparison has been right for long enough to believe. Nothing reads it any more.

title: One record of rank, taken on the hour

items.text: The snapshots file had three kinds of row in it: a daily snapshot, the same snapshot re-read later that day, and the per-refresh readings on top. The difference between them was an accident of the order they were built in, not anything about the data. They are all the same act, which is looking up somebody's rank and writing down what it said, so the file is now one log with one row shape.

Each row says why it exists, which is the only thing that really differed. A daily anchor is written once per player per queue per day whether or not anything moved, because the daily chart and the seven-day trend need a point on quiet days. Everything else is written because that player played that queue since their last reading.

That last part is new: a reading used to be kept whenever the number changed, and is now kept when somebody actually played. It is the same idea told properly, since LP only moves when a game is played, and it means the busiest player has the most rows. Gaps are still gaps on purpose. A rank that has not moved overnight has nothing to record, and the file says so rather than repeating itself two hundred times.

Readings are now taken on the hour instead of drifting. The rebuild used to happen once the published page was fifty-five minutes old, so each reading landed a little later than the last and the series slid around the clock, ending up at odd times like 32 minutes past. It now happens on the first trigger after the hour turns over, which is about two minutes past, every hour.

The readings log was being kept with the rebuildable caches, on a branch that is thrown away and rewritten from scratch every run. It is not rebuildable: Riot has no endpoint for a past rank, so one bad write there would have taken the record with it. It now lives beside the rank history, where every version is kept.
The old daily history is copied into the log so nothing from before per-refresh readings existed is lost, placed at exactly the times the charts already read those days at.

Each row now says why it is there in its own terms: a daily anchor, or played. Rows from before this was one log keep the rule they were written under rather than being relabelled as something they were not, so a reading carried over from the old daily file says end of day rather than claiming somebody played.

The step that carries the old daily file into the log was doing it for today as well, and today's row is re-stamped every run, so it added a row an hour to the file and would have turned the log back into the every-hour record it is deliberately not. It only carries finished days over now, and the duplicate rows the first couple of hours left behind are collapsed back to one per day.

title: Level on LP means level in the table

items.text: Two people on the same rank and the same LP now share a place on the leaderboard rather than one of them sitting arbitrarily above the other. The order between them was never a judgement about who was ahead; it was whichever way the sort happened to leave them, so the table was claiming something it did not know.

The place after a tie skips, the way a league table does: two people level on second are both second and the next one down is fourth. Skipping the third is the point, because it is what says there are two people above them rather than one. Tied players share the medal colour too, and their card carries the same number.

Being level is decided on the rank as shown, not on the single number the table sorts by. That number packs tier, division and LP together on a scale where a Master player's LP runs into the thousands, so two genuinely different ranks can land on the same figure. Good enough to sort by, not something to declare a tie on.
A refresh renumbers the table, and it now applies the same rule, including for anyone whose lookup failed: they hold the place the build gave them instead of dropping out of a tie they were part of.

title: Game times are on your clock now

items.text: Every game time on the page was printed in the timezone of the machine that built it, which is UTC, so all summer they read an hour early. The times now carry their timestamp and the browser rewrites them into your own clock when the page loads, the same way the 'Data from' stamp in the header already did. This covers the Recent Games list, the recent games table on each player's card, and the hover text on the little win and loss dots. A reader with JavaScript off still sees the UTC version rather than nothing.
The two downloadable text files are written when the page is built, so their times stay UTC. They say so at the top now.

Three more places where the browser rounded a half upwards and the page rounded it to the even neighbour, as Python does. One decides how often the LP chart labels its horizontal axis: with 135 games that works out at round(22.5), so the page numbered its games in twenty-twos and the browser in twenty-threes. Another is the winrate in the table under the chart, where a player sitting on exactly half a percent would have been a point apart. All of them go through the same rule now.

title: A date meant one instant on the server and another in your browser

items.text: The LP chart the page shipped and the LP chart your browser redrew after a refresh were built from the same data and did not agree. An old daily snapshot carries only a date, no time, and both sides turned that date into a timestamp in their own local time. The page is built on a UTC machine and read in a browser an hour ahead, so games played late on 19 August fell before the day's anchor on one side and after it on the other. Kirish's line had 133 games in the published chart and 135 after a refresh. Dates without a time are now read as UTC everywhere, which is what they have always meant, since snapshots are keyed by UTC day.

The merge that joins the hourly readings to the older daily ones was filtering by one clock and sorting by another: a daily anchor read in the morning was judged by the time its rank was last re-read that evening, and dropped. It now uses the same clock the chart itself is cut by.

With that fixed the two charts still differed by a tenth of a unit at one point out of several thousand. The padded top and bottom of the chart are worked out from the projection line's own floating point walk, and two runtimes need not agree on those to the last bit; that scales every coordinate by an invisible amount and flips whichever one happens to sit on a rounding boundary. The bounds are whole numbers now, which costs nothing on a padded axis and is the same number in both languages.

One more, and the one that was actually moving LP about. The browser's copy of Python's rounding rule treated any value within a billionth of a half as exactly a half, and sent it to the even neighbour. Neel's average win worked out to 17.499999999999996, three quadrillionths below the half and so a plain round down to 17 in the page; the tolerance called it a half and rounded to 18, so his twenty-sixth game was worth 23 LP on the page and 24 after a refresh. A double either sits on the half or it does not, and the test is exact now. The two charts are byte for byte identical again.

title: Recent Games is the last 100, and rank progress has three ranges

items.text: Recent Games listed every game since tracking began, which is the right thing to keep and the wrong thing to show: several hundred rows to scroll before reaching anything older than yesterday. It now shows the last 100 games. A game two friends played together counts once, not twice, so the hundred is a hundred games rather than a hundred rows.

A name row above the table. Pick anyone to see just their last 100 games, and a button appears to download their whole season as a text file: every ranked game they have played, in every queue, newest first.

Daily rank progress is three charts behind a toggle: the whole season, the last 30 days, and the last 7. A month is the right amount of detail for how the month has gone and the wrong amount for both of the other questions people ask of this chart, so each range now has its own axes rather than sharing one.

Readings from before a chart's window were pinned to its left edge instead of being left out, stacking a column of dots there. On a seven-day view that would have drawn the whole season as though it happened on the first day.
Date labels followed a fixed weekly step whatever the window, so the seven-day chart labelled its first day and then nothing until Today. Tick spacing now follows the span it is labelling.
Switching the LP chart's zoom un-highlighted the projection switch beside it, because the highlight moved across the whole panel rather than within the group that was clicked.

title: A game is worth what that player's games are worth

items.text: Per-game LP used a flat 20 as its starting point for everyone, so every step looked alike whoever played it. Each game is now worth what that player's wins and losses are actually worth, taken from their own record, with the remainder scattered so the segment still lands exactly on the measured rank. Winny's wins sit around 19 to 22, Neel's around 20 to 24, because that is what theirs are worth.

Which game absorbs a rounding remainder is chosen by the same seeded generator the projection line uses. It looks arbitrary, which it is, but it is the same arbitrary choice on every rebuild and in both the page and the browser's own redraw, so the graph does not shuffle underneath you.
MMR's recent window and the chart's zoomed view are both fifty games, sharing one constant.

title: The seven-day trend always has a number now

items.text: A gap in the rank history erased the trend entirely. With no readings between 30 August and 2 September, the nearest reading to seven days ago was 28.6 hours away, four hours outside the window the rule allowed, so every row read insufficient data. Meanwhile the page's own refresh button had no such rule and cheerfully showed a number, so two parts of the page disagreed. The nearest reading is now always used.

The tilde says how far off it was: 29 hours from exactly seven days ago, rather than just that it was approximate. That is the difference between knowing whether to trust the figure and only knowing that you should not fully.
Insufficient data now means what it says: fewer than two readings, so there is nothing to compare. A player who genuinely has not moved still shows a dash, which is a different answer again.

title: LP per game is measured hourly, not smoothed over a day

items.text: Rank was recorded once a day, so a day's games all fell in one gap and the LP change across it was divided between them by formula. On a heavy evening that was thirty games sharing a single measurement, which is why individual steps on the graph did not match what anyone remembered playing. A reading is now recorded on every refresh, and the LP between two readings is split only between the games actually played between them. In testing that took the worst case from 32 games per measurement to 1.

Segments are cut by timestamp rather than by calendar day. A reading with no timestamp, from before readings were kept, is placed at the end of its day, which is where a once-daily evening snapshot actually sat. The daily chart still reads the midnight snapshots and is unaffected.

Readings that repeat the previous value are not stored: an identical reading says only that nobody played since, and keeping those would triple the file to record nothing. Three weeks are kept, which covers the seven day trend and the recent part of the per-game chart.

The daily chart's line ended at this morning's midnight reading while the table beside it showed the live rank, so for anyone who had played since midnight the two disagreed: Rory's line finished 41 LP from the number printed next to it. Past days keep their midnight anchor, which is what makes them comparable; today plots where the player actually is.

title: A seven-day trend says when it is not quite seven days

items.text: Where the nearest rank reading is more than two hours from seven days ago, the trend is marked with a tilde and says so on hover. The number is real; the period behind it is approximate, and that was previously silent.

Where there is no reading within a day of seven days ago, the trend reads insufficient data rather than a dash. A dash meant nothing moved, which is a different answer from nothing could be measured, and reaching further back to fill the gap would put a stale comparison under a seven day heading.

title: An L on the logo

items.text: The header mark is an L rather than the two chevrons. It is drawn rather than copied: Riot's fan content policy is happy with fan projects and unhappy with their trademark being used as somebody else's branding, which is what a site logo is.

title: Download the LP working as a text file

items.text: A Download as .txt button under Recent Games on the LP per game panel. It gives every reconstructed game with the LP worked out for it and the rank it left the player on, plus the measured snapshots the whole reconstruction is anchored on, and a note on each row saying whether it landed on a real reading or was part of a split.

The file is written by the generator and carried in the page rather than assembled in the browser. It exists to check the arithmetic, and rebuilding it in a second language would mean auditing the maths with another copy of the maths.

title: A suspended account is marked as one

items.text: A red line across a suspended account, on the leaderboard row and on their card. The detail sits in the hover text rather than on the page.
It is a date in the config rather than a flag, so it lifts by itself. Nothing checks for bans and nothing could: Riot does not expose that. Somebody types the date.

title: The rank beside the LP chart was stuck at midnight

items.text: Anchoring the daily snapshot to midnight, so the Daily rank progress chart compares like with like, had a consequence I missed: every other thing reading that history got this morning's rank instead of the current one. The table under the LP per game chart showed Kirish on Emerald III 30 LP when he was on 10, beside a game list refreshing every hour.

Worse, the per-game chart was forcing today's games to land on that midnight reading, which is a rank measured before they were played. The line was being dragged backwards to meet it. Each day's row now keeps both readings: the midnight anchor the daily chart wants, and the latest one, refreshed every run, that the per-game chart and the standings need.

title: Replacing the Riot key now updates the website too

items.text: set_key.py only ever changed the copy on your PC. The published site is built on GitHub, which reads the key from a repository secret and never sees config.json, so replacing an expired key locally left the website failing exactly as before. It now sets the secret as well, and says plainly what to do if it cannot.
It also stopped telling you to run the local publish script afterwards, which has not been how the site updates since it moved to GitHub.

title: Exes was counting Flex and 5s

items.text: Exes was the only card in the duo panel not restricted to Ranked Solo/Duo. The five others come from the same Solo/Duo figures as the matrix, but Exes read the duo lookup directly, and that covers all three ranked queues because it also tints the With column on a match list where any shared game counts. It answered Rory and Winny at 14 days; the Solo/Duo answer is Neel and Shas at 58.

title: Every highlight now shows its working

items.text: Each of the 39 highlight cards has a How this was worked out link. Opening it gives the measurement in a sentence and the full standings behind it: everyone who was measured, in order, with the gap to whoever won. A card asserting somebody is the best at something invites exactly one question, and the numbers to answer it were already being computed and thrown away.

The standings also name who could not be measured and why, because not on the list and last on the list mean very different things. Someone with 12 games where the card needs 20 is absent for a reason that is worth stating.

The games column is labelled Season games on the season cards, and the five cards that can only measure part of a season say so explicitly. The wall, The assassin, Diffed, Besto Friendo and the vision card depend on fields recorded only on recently fetched matches, so the season total beside their numbers is not the sample they were taken over.

The disclosure arrow rendered as a control character followed by the literal text b8. It was written as the CSS escape for a triangle, but the whole stylesheet lives inside a Python f-string and Python reads a backslash followed by digits as an octal escape long before CSS sees it. The character is written directly now.

The working table no longer runs off the edge of a card on a phone. The unit is written once in the column heading rather than after all seven numbers, the word behind moved into the heading too, and the table scrolls in place if a long name still beats a narrow card.

A change to the page itself now publishes straight away instead of waiting for the data to go stale. The publish gate measures how old the data is, which is right for data and wrong for code: a fix would sit unpublished for up to an hour while the gate correctly reported nothing about the data had changed, which looked exactly like the deploy being broken. The page now carries a fingerprint of the generator that built it, and the gate rebuilds when that no longer matches.

title: Publishing four times an hour to publish once, and a key countdown

items.text: The hourly publish was not hourly. GitHub's scheduler is a queue rather than a clock, and on a public repo it does not merely run late: an hourly trigger produced runs at 16:21, 19:39 and 22:29 one evening, three of the eight it owed, leaving the page nearly two hours old. The schedule now fires every fifteen minutes and a gate job reads the live page first, doing the work only when what a visitor can actually see is more than fifty-five minutes old. An hour is missed only if all four triggers are dropped.

A chip in the header saying when the Riot API key was added and how long it has left, counting down in the browser so a page left open overnight does not keep claiming hours it no longer has. It turns amber under six hours and red under one. Set api_key_permanent in config.json and it says the key does not expire instead.

set_key.py stamps the key's clock when the key is installed rather than leaving it to the next fetch. A key pasted in the evening would otherwise be dated to whenever the schedule next ran, and a countdown wrong in the optimistic direction is worse than no countdown.

The key chip printed its times in the builder's timezone rather than the reader's. The page is built by a GitHub runner on UTC and read from the UK, so a key added at 13:00 was shown to everybody as 12:00. Both times are now carried as timestamps and formatted in the browser.

Data from is shown in your own timezone, with how long ago that was. The page is built by a GitHub runner on UTC, so through British Summer Time a reader in the UK was shown a time an hour behind their own clock and the page looked an hour more stale than it was. It sat next to a key countdown that had just been fixed to use local time, so the header was quietly running two clocks.

title: Cards in a declared order, and a KDA term that finally counts

items.text: Every card panel now reads in a fixed order, three to a row, rather than in whatever order the code happened to build them. The grid is pinned to three columns too: it used to fit two, three or four across depending on the window, so the rows the cards were grouped into were only sometimes the rows on screen.

Top champions weighted a champion's KDA against the account's own average, but the term only reached its full six points at double or half that average, which nobody manages. In practice a six point term never moved past one. A third above or below now scores full value, so KDA changes the order instead of decorating it.

A champion needs 10 games to be a top champion. The old floor was three, and it was dropped entirely whenever it could not otherwise fill five rows, which was exactly when the thin records deserved least trust. Some players will show fewer than five champions now; that is the honest answer rather than a padded one.
Games this week is Total games this week, Most active is Most active player, and Played together is Games played together. Animal of the week counts people rather than of them.

New icons for Sisyphus, Total games this week, Unemployed, Tickle monster, Passenger, Resilient and Diffed. The two that were broken, a rock and a palm-down hand, were both recent Unicode additions, which is exactly when a glyph turns into an empty box on somebody's phone.
Rory is steel again and Brett is back on copper. They sit next to each other in every legend, so only one of the two can be a warm colour without the pair reading as one.

title: Highlight cards reworded, and two of them were lying

items.text: The wall and The assassin were reporting nonsense: 239 damage soaked per death, 53 damage per takedown. Damage taken is only recorded on matches fetched since that field was added, about 3% of the season, but the totals were being divided by every match's deaths. A partial numerator over a complete denominator. Both now measure across the same matches, and read 4,376 and 1,289.
The assassin: whoever takes the least damage for each kill or assist they get. Dealing death without being hit.

Rank progress (last 30 days) is now Daily rank progress, and its reading is taken at midnight GMT rather than whenever the machine happened to be on. Every point on that chart is now a comparable time of day. Rank now beside it reads the live standing, so it does not go stale between midnights.

Data from now names the moment the run started asking Riot rather than the moment it finished writing. The fetch takes about seventy seconds, so an hourly job firing at 15:00:02 was reporting its data as 15:01:14, which read like it had missed the hour.

Grasshopper asked for a champion never played this season, which ruled out anyone coming back to something after a long gap. It now wants one untouched in the previous seven days that was under 5% of their picks before that.
Passenger measures the lowest KDA in games won, not games lost. A low KDA in a game you lost is just losing; a low KDA in a game your team won anyway is being carried.

Rory takes the orange and Brett the steel. They sit next to each other in every legend, so orange beside copper read as one colour. Shas and Shas2nd are now two shades of the same pink, being two accounts belonging to one person.

Keep coming up short is now Resilient. Sisyphus had a boulder emoji that rendered as an empty box on Windows. Biggest climber names the LP and both ranks and drops the winrate. Played together, Animal of the week, Most loved champion, The DPS, Tickle monster, Dirty KSer, On a mission, Int alert, Speedrunner, Diffed, Vegas wedding and Sneaky link have all been reworded.
The assassin and The wall now sit together, the vision card follows Int alert, Besto Friendo follows Speedrunner, and Healthy relationship follows Perfect couple.
The Hot streak badge is gone from the friend cards. The busiest day tile now reads as a sentence: the number, then games played on that day.

Only Ranked Solo/Duo, Flex and 5s can reach a stat, and the build now prints the count of each so the mix is visible rather than assumed. Anything else is dropped and reported loudly. Teamfight Tactics is a separate game on a separate API that nothing here calls, so it has no route into the data in the first place; this is the third gate rather than the first.

title: Publishing on the hour, and two-colour duo cards

items.text: The scheduled publish now runs on the hour rather than on whatever minute the task happened to be created. Every run fetches from Riot, rebuilds and deploys, so the whole page is at most an hour old, cards and totals included.

The tier bands were missing from the Rank progress chart. The two charts do not plot the same scale: the LP chart plots ladder position, four divisions of a hundred LP, while this one plots a tier score of a thousand a tier. The bands were being drawn on the LP chart's scale and landed nowhere near the right ranks.
The duo cards sit below the grid, and each one carries both players' colours: the first named at the top, the second at the bottom, blended through the middle.

title: Rory is steel blue

items.text: Rory takes the steel blue that was sitting unused at the end of the palette. His slot sits beside Brett's in every legend, and orange next to copper read as one colour at a glance.

title: Season highlights, week tiles and duo cards

items.text: A Season highlights panel: MVP, KDA king, Farm god, Marathon day, Season grinder, Unemployed, Chicken dinner, If at first you don't succeed, Sisyphus, The DPS, Tickle monster, Dirty KSer, On a mission, Int alert, Passenger, Keep coming up short, Speedrunner, Lights were too bright and Just this once. Each names a winner, the number behind it, and enough detail to see why.

This week at a glance is rebuilt: games and hours this week, most active player, games played together, biggest climber with winrate and LP, hottest streak, animal of the week, most loved champion, adaptable and grasshopper. A tile about the group needs two or more players in it, so a champion one person spammed cannot be the group's most loved.
Six cards under the duo grid: Lovers, Perfect couple, Vegas wedding, Healthy relationship, Exes and Sneaky link.
A table of the ten highest rated champion performances anywhere in the group, with the player, the rating, the games and the winrate.

fetch_data.py now records damage taken, vision score, the lane opponent's own KDA, the surrender flag, and the champions of everyone else on the team. Four highlights are waiting on those and stay hidden until a --refetch-details pass fills them in, rather than showing a number they cannot support.

title: Real champion names, tier bands, and a schedule that publishes itself

items.text: update_and_publish.ps1 fetches, rebuilds and publishes in one go, and setup_auto_update.ps1 can put it on a half-hourly, hourly, three-hourly or daily schedule. This is the only thing that moves the numbers a shared link shows: the Refresh button runs in the viewer's own browser with the viewer's own key and writes nothing back, because the site is a static file with no server behind it.

Champion names with spaces were printed as Riot's internal key: Nunu, MissFortune, KSante. They read as Nunu & Willump, Miss Fortune and K'Sante now, everywhere including tooltips and the browser's own redraws.
The face on a card was a square in a circle. It sits in a frame that clips it now, and is scaled past that frame so the border Data Dragon draws inside every champion square is cropped away.
Both rank charts have a wash of each tier's own colour behind them, so a line's height reads as a rank without tracking back to the axis.
The 7 day trend follows a live rank now, on the leaderboard and on each card. It measures from the last reading seven days back, which does not move, to whatever rank is being shown.

A player keeps their colour when the ladder moves under them. Colours were handed out by rank, so a promotion swapped two people's colours on every chart, table and tint; they now follow the order in the config. Rory is orange.
Solo and Duo are one hue with Duo the weaker of the two, since they are the same queue counted two ways. Flex and 5s are separate queues and now have separate hues: magenta and amber.

KDA counts toward a champion's rating, measured against that player's own average across every game rather than an absolute, so a champion they play better than they usually play is worth more than one they merely win on. The champion pool table shows KDA as a column.
A KDA gap under 0.25 is no longer marked as carrying the pair. Thirteen marks become five.
The (est.) tag is off the LP column: every step between two snapshots is reconstructed, so tagging nearly all of them said nothing. The tint on a refreshed row is gone too.

title: Ring seams, and a palette per queue and per role

items.text: The ring segments overlapped at their edges. Each arc was drawn as a dash pattern of "this segment, then the rest of the circle", and those two numbers were rounded separately, so the pattern came out about seven ten-thousandths short of the circumference. A dash pattern repeats, so every arc wrapped and painted a sliver of itself back over the start of the ring. The gap is now a whole circumference, which can never come round, and each segment starts on the exact sum of the ones before it.

Roles have their own colours: Top red, Jungle green, Mid blue, ADC yellow, Support orange, all pulled down and desaturated so none can be mistaken for a winrate or a friend's identity colour. Bottom is labelled ADC.

Game types are two families: Solo Queue violet with Duo Queue a lighter violet, Ranked Flex teal with Ranked 5s a lighter teal. The winrate bars on each card take the colour their queue has in the ring above them.
A player's face was drawn 42 pixels wide inside a 44 pixel circle, because the ring around it was a border and a border sits inside the box. The ring is a shadow now, so the art fills the circle.
Faces and card art are the champion played most this season. A face should be what you would actually see them on.
The counter pick tag is off the Top champions table. It still marks the matchups it describes.

title: Shorter names

items.text: The collapsible sections are named for what they hold rather than described: Recent Games, Daily Changes, Ranked Pairs, and on each card Most Recent Games, Champion Pool and Champion Matchups. The counts come off the headings, since the tables state their own length.
The game types ring reads Duo Queue, Solo Queue, Ranked Flex and Ranked 5s.

title: The 5s bar draws, and a counter pick has to earn the name

items.text: The Ranked 5s bar was empty. It asked for a colour variable that was never defined, so its gradient did not parse and the fill had nothing to draw with.
The strip down the side of each Overview card is that player's own colour, the same one they carry on the charts and in the duo grid. Cards about the group rather than a person keep the house accent.

The corner mark in the duo grid is sized by how far ahead the carrying player is, scaled against the widest gap in the group, so the marks rank as well as flag. Brett and Winny is the widest at the moment.

A counter pick now has to pass three tests: the champion is played a tenth of the time or less, so a main can never be one; the matchup wins outright at 60% or better; and the margin over that player's own winrate clears what a run that short could produce by chance. Two matchups qualify across the group, where the old rule tagged Zed on 423 games.
The coverage table under Trios and five mans is gone.

title: Ranked 5s is in, and every game now knows its lane

items.text: Ranked 5s is imported: 172 games across six players, with a ladder rank for each. Riot calls that ladder RANKED_PREMADE_5x5 and the queue 710. It has its own row on every card, its own slice in the game types ring, its own column in the champion table, and it counts toward the five-man stacks.

Lane data is complete. Every one of the 2,713 games now records the position played and the champion in the opposing lane, where before only 171 did. Kirish's matchup table goes from nothing to 43 entries and the roles ring is built from every game rather than one in seventeen.
Remakes are Riot's own call now rather than a guess from game length. The duration rule was cutting games Riot does not consider remakes at all.
Rank snapshots cover Ranked 5s as well as Solo/Duo and Flex, so its trend, its peak and its LP per win will build up the same way the others did.

1,953 cache entries under the original match-id-only key are gone. Nothing could read them: every lookup is matchId|puuid, which is what stops two friends in the same game from overwriting each other's stat line.

title: A seven day trend that covers seven days

items.text: The 7 day trend kept only the snapshots that fell inside the window, which measures whatever happened to land there rather than the window itself. With readings on the 21st, 27th and 29th it compared the 27th against the 29th and called two days a week: Shas2nd showed no movement at all despite a demotion, and a fifty LP drop earlier in the week did not register. It now anchors on the last reading at or before the cutoff, which is what the rank actually was seven days ago. Shas2nd reads -42 LP and a demotion; Kirish -53; Brett +119.
The leaderboard's trend column drops the (7d) suffix, which repeated its own heading.
The header says "Data from" and its build time, and a live refresh appends when the ranks on top of it were read. The build time only moves when fetch_data.py runs, which is what a shared link shows.

fetch_data.py --prune-cache drops the 1,953 cache entries left under the original match-id-only key. Nothing can read them: every lookup uses matchId|puuid, which is what stops two friends in the same game from overwriting each other's stat line.

A --refetch-details pass that could not re-fetch a match kept the cached copy instead of dropping the game. Riot stops serving very old matches, and losing a game from the season to gain a field on it is the wrong trade.

title: Faces follow the top champion, and the key follows the live ladder

items.text: The LP per game key and the standings under it kept the order the page was published in, so after a refresh somebody who had dropped to 0 LP still sat above somebody on 26. Both now sort on the rank they are showing. The chart's own lines keep their published order, because that is what ties a line to a colour.

The rank crests are not drawn to one scale: the tier ones sit inside a 20x20 box with a margin, unranked fills a 16x16 box edge to edge, and gold is 17x13. Unranked is scaled back to the weight of a tier crest and all of them fit rather than stretch.

The queue bars started and finished at different points because the column holding the record was sized to its text, so a queue reading 0W / 0L gave the bar beside it more room than one reading 447W / 446L. Fixed width now.
The 7 day trend is Ranked Solo/Duo only, with no queue letters.
A game added by a refresh is no longer tinted blue. It fought with the shared-game colour on the same row, and a new game is a game like any other.
A card's face and background art are the top of its weighted champion table rather than highest mastery, so the picture and the table agree. Winny is Twitch rather than Samira.

The duo grid marks the corner of a cell where the player on that row holds the higher KDA across the pair's games, so reading across a row shows which pairings they carry. The KDA comparison is Solo/Duo only now, matching the grid it sits in.

Hovering "weighted" on a card spells out the rating: the player's own winrate, plus the champion's lift shrunk by games / (games + 15) and halved for its counter-pick share, plus up to 16 points for volume.

title: Ranked 5s on the cards, and rank colours that match their crests

items.text: Ranked 5s has its own row on every friend card and its own slice in the game types ring. A queue with no ladder entry still shows its record, counted off the season's own games.

Diamond's text was blue while its crest is violet. Every rank colour is now taken from the mini crest the page draws next to it. Diamond keeps the bluer half of the violet range and Master the redder, so the two stay apart in a leaderboard.
An unranked crest, so an unranked queue gets the same treatment as a ranked one instead of an empty square.

The 7 day trend used a hollow triangle for "nothing recorded", which is still an arrow shape: a card with two quiet queues read as two upward arrows. It is a grey dash now. Direction is settled first (green up for LP gained, red down for LP lost, grey dash for nothing), and only then does the distance decide the count. Each queue's group is tagged S, F or 5, since two untagged groups side by side read as one run of arrows about one thing.
Top champions and Highest mastery now share a row height, so the two tables line up down the card.
A card's face and background art are the player's highest mastery champion.

The refresh had a budget of 40 match lookups for the whole group, which a seven person list can exhaust partway down, leaving whoever came last with nothing and making it look as though only one person had played. Everyone gets their full window now, and the status line names who got new games rather than only counting them.
The Fresh badge is gone from the cards, and the snapshot count is gone from the rank progress table.

title: Ranked 5s found, and the cards lose their footnotes

items.text: Ranked 5s is queue 710. Of the three unnamed queue ids sitting in the match cache it is the only one played on Summoner's Rift at all, with a real CS per minute on all 34 of its games where every game under 1740 and 1750 has none. All 34 fall on a Friday, Saturday or Sunday and all 34 start between 19:00 and 23:59. It is back on the fetch list, so those games will import on the next run.
The ring charts have no key underneath. Hovering a segment puts its count, its share and its name in the middle of the ring instead.
The 7 day trend is one to three arrows: one up to 50 LP, two to 100, three beyond, green up or red down, one group per queue.
Rank emblems sit outside the text in the card's top corner, so the current and peak crests line up down the edge.
The four season figures run in a line above the champion tables, which gives the weighted table room enough to read without sliding it sideways.
Every champion, most played first now splits its games by queue, so a total can be checked against a site that counts a different set of them.
The paragraphs explaining how each number was worked out are gone from the page.

title: Friend cards rebuilt, and 64 remakes stop counting as games

items.text: 64 remakes were counting as real games. fetch_data.py drops them, but only for matches fetched since it started reading Riot's early-surrender flag, and 2,396 of 2,565 records here predate that. They are now spotted by duration: nothing but a remake ends inside four minutes, and there is a clean gap between the three minute remakes and the six minute stomps. Kirish's season drops from 971 games to 946 and his Zed from 401 to 393.

LP per win and per loss was wrong. It solved for one pair of numbers across every snapshot gap at once, and a single gap that could not be squared with the rest dragged the whole answer: Brett came out at 13.4 LP a loss when he actually loses about 19. It now reads the per-game steps the LP chart is already drawn from, which are fitted to land exactly on each measured snapshot. Brett is 22.0 and 18.3, and 20 wins and 8 losses at those rates comes to the +294 LP his rank really moved.

A game added by a refresh was built with eight cells where the table has nine: the "With" column was missing entirely, so every column from Champion rightwards landed one place left of its own heading. Those rows now also carry the shared-game tint, and are written only once every friend has been fetched, since a game two of them played is only recognisable as shared once both fetches are back.

Friend cards rebuilt. The ranked queues read down the left with their winrate bars, and two ring charts on the right show what the season was made of: which queue each game was played in, with Solo/Duo split by whether one of the group was on the team, and which lane it was played from. Under them, the weighted champion table, the mastery table and the season tiles sit side by side, then LP per win and per loss for every queue over the season and the last 20 games. The card header carries a trend arrow per queue.
A switch to turn the projected lines on the LP per game chart off.

Under the stacks table, an account of where everyone's Flex and Ranked 5s games went: how many were in a listed trio or five man, how many had four of them on a team (a five man whose fifth player is outside the group, since Flex has no four player party), and how many had only one or two of them. The three add up to the total, so Rory playing 28 Flex games and appearing in rows worth 18 of them is explained rather than looking like a gap.

fetch_data.py kept only RANKED_SOLO_5x5 and RANKED_FLEX_SR from Riot's ranked entries and discarded anything else. Every queue Riot returns is now carried through under its own name, and any queue in a match history that has no name yet is printed, so a ranked queue that exists can no longer be invisible.

title: A live rank reading reaches the whole page

items.text: Refreshing updated the leaderboard and nothing else. The rank in each card's top corner, the Solo/Duo row underneath it with its winrate bar and record, the card's accent colour, and the "Rank now" column under the LP chart all kept showing whatever was true when the page was built, so one screen gave two different answers to the same question. They all follow the live reading now.
The "Rank now" column only updated when the refresh also found new games, because the live reading was only fed to the chart alongside them. It is applied on its own now.
A live rank above anything on record is treated as the new peak, instead of printing a current rank with a lower peak underneath it.
